newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Envoys stand by tougher policy on Bosnian fugitives.
newsitem.headline: Envoys stand by tougher policy on Bosnian fugitives.

text.p: Western peace coordinators in Bosnia vowed on Tuesday to stand firm behind a tougher international approach to indicted war criminals despite Russian criticism of a NATO arrest operation last week and two apparently retaliatory bombings.

A spokesman for the High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, made clear that Western governments were not considering a "climbdown" when it came to extraditing those indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

"I think it highly unlikely that once we set this train in motion that it's going to be stopped nor would the office of the High Representative wish to see it stopped," Duncan Bullivant, spokesman for Westendorp, told reporters.
"The removal of indicted war criminals from the playing field and their appearance in The Hague is the only way to guarantee the success of the Dayton peace agreement."

Two bombings in two days apparently targeting international monitors caused no injuries but raised the spectre of a possible backlash in Bosnia's Serb republic against a more aggressive posture by NATO towards suspected war criminals.
U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Bosnian Serbs against taking revenge for the NATO raid on two Serb suspects.
"They have no call to take any retaliatory action and it would be a grave mistake to do so," Clinton told reporters in Washington.
Russia, supporting their Serb allies, has criticised the alliance for carrying out what it called "cowboy raids" against two Serb suspects charged by the tribunal.
One suspect was detained last Thursday and another shot dead after he opened fire on British soldiers.
Westendorp, who oversees the civilian side of Bosnia's 1995 peace agreement, was due to hold talks with Russian officials in an attempt to allay Moscow's concerns over the NATO swoop.
Russia has a troop contingent in the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission said the bombing of an OSCE truck on Sunday night and a smaller explosion outside the apartment of an OSCE monitor on Monday night in Serb territory were "troubling".

Spokesman David Foley said the incidents were still under investigation but the OSCE remained committed to seeing suspected war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic, face trial before the tribunal.
"We do not modify our positions because of this sort of activity," Foley said.

The OSCE, which is organising post-war elections in Bosnia, has angered nationalist hardliners loyal to Karadzic for striking some of their candidates from electoral lists due to reports of fraudulent voter registration.
SFOR has reported no reprisals against its heavily-armed soldiers since the raid against indicted war criminals in the northwest town of Prijedor, near Banja Luka.
NATO has refused to rule out more arrests and the existence of sealed, or secret, indictments like the ones used in the swoop last week fed rumours and speculation about who might be next.
The two most prominent suspects on the published list of indictments are Karadzic and his former army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
Both men, charged with crimes against humanity, have often been seen in Serb-controlled areas of Bosnia and in neighbouring Serbian-led Yugoslavia.

The U.N. tribunal said legal proceedings for Milan Kovacevic, who was arrested last Thursday by British soldiers on charges of complicity in a genocidal campaign against Moslems and Croats, would have to be delayed because doctors discovered he was physically ill.

Kovacevic underwent a medical examination after his arrival in The Hague during which "the doctor discovered the existence of pathological problems which call for the accused to be placed under supervision," the tribunal said in a statement.
